Jeff asked for a way to amend old plans from the TUI, meaning edit them literally, as a test of the draft as a way to weigh an idea. The draft planned the feature properly, said Claude's view up front (the wrong tool), and marked each place the feature overturned earlier ground. Its one prompt defaulted to building it, because an agent doesn't get a veto. Jeff answered in his own words at the second entry, and this plan records that answer as a decline. What he wants instead, asking for a plan to be revisited, is its own draft.

Decline: Editing a landed plan from the TUI

Anchored by tarlatan, Decision: A request to revisit is a notes file on a landed plan, kept in drafts/.

where internal/tui/screens.go file page

quote m.status = "only a draft takes notes; a plan is testimony"

Because (Jeff): "If anything can be considered immutable, it has to be the plans - so the tui should not allow you to edit them. It is a Ulysses mast move - I could always edit them outside of this tool, but damn... that would be a bad idea." And: what was wrong with "edit" was "I want to do this behind your back, Claude", not "let's have a conversation around this." The draft found five collisions, any one of which would have been a revisit:

  • The TUI's own rule, which stays as it is: only a draft takes notes, and a plan is testimony.
  • next.md: the TUI's one write is a draft's notes file, and it never writes the substrate. A landed plan is what the substrate is generated from.
  • An edit lands in whatever commit comes next, and phoropter shows the new words under the plan's original date and added commit.
  • A plan page carries no hash of its file, so the TUI couldn't check it was editing the version just read.
  • The annotating agreement: whoever annotates a file doesn't edit it. Most plans here were written by Claude from drafts Jeff annotated, and batiste declined even converting a draft from the TUI.

Nothing on the site would show a plan had changed: phoropter reads plans as written, and the TUI reads no git history. A reader, and an agent reading the page, would take the edited words as what was decided. Changing a landed plan's ground stays what the guide says it is: a revisit, in a new plan that cites the old one.
